context_blurb:
When COVID-19 swept the world in 2020, officials had to act fast on thin evidence, and scientists split over what to do. Studies and released records now let anyone weigh some of those choices and see where experts still disagree.

In October 2020 Harvard's Martin Kulldorff, Oxford's Sunetra Gupta and Stanford's Jay Bhattacharya put their names to the Great Barrington Declaration. They called their plan Focused Protection: shield the old and frail, who faced the greatest danger, and let the young and healthy return to normal life, schools included. It never proposed letting the virus sweep through every age alike. Critics answered in The Lancet that keeping so many people apart for long was impractical, and that spread among the young would reach everyone.

Francis Collins, who ran the National Institutes of Health, judged the plan dangerous. Four days after the signing, Collins emailed Anthony Fauci that the declaration's premises needed a quick and devastating published takedown, calling its authors "three fringe epidemiologists". A records request made the email public in 2021. In 2023 Collins called the three "very distinguished" and regretted some of his words, while holding that the plan would have cost lives.

Sweden never shut its preschools or its schools for children under sixteen that spring. Jonas Ludvigsson's team checked the records of all of Sweden's nearly two million children aged one to sixteen over those months. Not one had died of COVID-19, and 15 had needed intensive care, about one child in 130,000. The study did not measure whether children carried the virus home.

Anna Eva Hallin's team studied the reading tests of some 97,000 Swedish pupils in the first three grades and found that during the pandemic their reading was no worse than before, even among pupils from poorer homes. Even so, sickness and short closures upset teaching in about a third of Swedish schools.

Officials closed schools in 2020 as a precaution, following influenza models in which the young drive spread, while the new disease's risk to children was still unknown. When Stanford's Sean Reardon and Harvard's Thomas Kane matched local scores to time spent in remote school, they found bigger losses where districts stayed online longer, but many districts back in person lost ground too. They cautioned that remote districts may have differed in other ways too.

In January 2023 Tom Jefferson's Cochrane review of randomised trials found community mask-wearing probably made little or no difference to illnesses like flu or COVID. Its editor-in-chief, Karla Soares-Weiser, said in March that "masks don't work" was a misleading reading. The trials, she explained, tested whether urging people to wear masks slowed the spread, comparing groups urged to wear them with groups that were not. In the largest, only 42.3 percent of the mask group wore one, against 13.3 percent of the others.

The Lancet critics of October 2020 had also found no evidence yet of lasting protection after infection, when the disease was under a year old. By 2023 the COVID-19 Forecasting Team could pool sixty-five studies. Forty weeks after an infection, protection against severe illness was still high, near 90 percent, while protection against catching it again was falling, to about 36 percent for one newer form of the virus.

Three economists, Steve Hanke, Lars Jonung and Jonas Herby, pooled studies of deaths under the spring 2020 lockdowns in Europe and America. Their first estimate, in January 2022, was a fall in deaths of 0.2 percent; a revised version, later a book, raised it to 3.2 percent. Both figures set deaths under strict, legally required rules against deaths under lighter, more voluntary ones such as Sweden's, not against doing nothing. Seth Flaxman of Oxford objected that the review left out every study built on the science of how disease spreads.

Where the disease came from is still unsettled. In February 2020, 27 public-health scientists in The Lancet rejected any suggestion of an unnatural origin; about three in four new human diseases were then known to come from animals. In 2023 the FBI leaned toward a lab accident with moderate confidence, and the Energy Department agreed with low confidence, while four other agencies leaned toward animals, also with low confidence. In January 2025 the CIA, undecided in 2021 and 2023, judged a lab accident likelier but held this view with low confidence, saying both origins remain plausible.

In April 2025 Jay Bhattacharya, a declaration author, became the eighteenth director to lead the National Institutes of Health, the main US agency for medical research.
